prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks

statement.case_for: After reading the opening ballots I move B005 from second to first place in my own ordering. It has the broadest backing in the room (five top-three placements, two first places, and a place on seven of the eight ballots) and it survives the tests I care most about as an instrumentalist. The invention is clean and original: magic-wavelength trapping lets many atoms be interrogated at once without a first-order light shift, and that single idea is why fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 became reachable. The result has been independently reproduced and surpassed in several countries and species, so it does not depend on one collaboration. It is also a measurement-science advance with downstream consequences (relativistic geodesy, constraints on varying constants, the pending redefinition of the second). Attribution is unusually tidy for the supplied names: Katori for the concept and first realization, Ye for taking performance and systematic control to the frontier. Two laureates, one idea, no collaboration-size problem.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the prize would partly honour a precision-measurement programme whose headline payoff, the redefinition of the second, has not yet happened, and that the frequency-comb and ultracold-atom lineage (Hall, Hansch, Wineland, Ketterle) already carries earlier prizes, so the committee may be asked whether this is a distinct achievement or an incremental refinement. Strontium and ytterbium lattice clocks also share credit with ion clocks (Al+ and others) that reach comparable accuracy by a different route, and a citation that is too broad could blur that. Finally, I ranked B035 first on opening, and B005 competes with it only in the sense that the committee has many mature options and I should not let my own field proximity decide.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B005 first because lattice clocks combine laser cooling, magic-wavelength trapping and ultrastable lasers to reach 1e-18 well beyond microwave standards, with replication in many laboratories.
responses.response: I agree on the science and have moved toward your ordering. I would add one qualification: the 'distinct from earlier prizes' argument has to be made explicitly, since the comb work and the 2012 ion-control prize are in the background. I think it is made by the magic-wavelength idea itself, which is Katori's and not part of those earlier citations, and I would keep the citation tied to the lattice clock invention rather than to 'precision time' in general so it does not read as a second prize for the same lineage.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene (B014) first, as a theory prediction of magic-angle flat bands followed by experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity, and notes strong replication.
responses.response: I take B014 seriously and keep it as my first alternative: the theory-plus-experiment pairing is real and the field is very large. My disagreement is about maturity and attribution. The microscopic origin of the superconductivity is still debated, so a citation would have to stay with the observation of correlated states and not their explanation, and the credited trio leaves out junior experimental co-discoverers, and the experimental field is only about eight years old. I would not put it ahead of a result whose interpretation has been stable for two decades, but I would not resist it if the committee judges the concept already settled.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs observation (B055) first as the experimental counterpart to the 2013 theory prize, while conceding that credit across two collaborations and the machine is the hard part.
responses.response: I agree that B055 is scientifically beyond doubt, and I share the difficulty you identify. A prize can name at most three people, and any trio drawn from Gianotti, Evans, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee leaves out at least two others whose roles are comparable, plus thousands of collaborators. That is a legitimate reason to hesitate and not a reason to dismiss. It is why I am not putting it first, but I would want the committee to say clearly whether it considers an incomplete trio acceptable, because B005 does not face that problem at all.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the KPZ universality class (B016) first as an organizing concept in non-equilibrium statistical physics, but flags that Parisi is not among the credited names.
responses.response: The conceptual depth is clear and the experimental realizations in liquid-crystal turbulence are a real strength. The attribution gap you note is serious for me: without Parisi the core of the 1986 paper is incomplete, and the supplied three-name credit makes Spohn the third laureate on the basis of mathematical later work. I would want the committee to resolve whether a KPZ prize can be justified with this credit list before treating it as competitive with B005.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer to pair the lattice clock with a second achievement in a two-part prize is unresolved; the credit limit of three people makes most pairings with a three-name candidate infeasible.
The exact framing of the B005 citation relative to ion clocks and earlier frequency-metrology prizes.
Whether the unrealized redefinition of the second should weigh as a maturity concern or merely as a pending application.
For B035, I have not verified how adequately the supplied names represent the DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA pioneers; this stays a judgment call.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B005. For astroparticle candidates such as B035 my professional connections (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGO+ and XL-Calibur collaborations, KTH astroparticle group) are in an adjacent field and not with IceCube as documented, but the committee should know of the field proximity if B035 is advanced.
